title: Burdzy-Scheutzow Problem 7.5 (our id P0032): PROVED - a random prefix turns any absolutely continuous process into Brownian motion
body:
Burdzy and Scheutzow, Forward Brownian motion (arXiv:1302.6958), Problem 7.5 (p. 26) asks: for any process {X_t, t >= 0} whose law is equivalent to Brownian motion, can one find a random piece to put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion? Our result (id P0032, 2026-09-08): YES - and under absolute continuity rather than equivalence, which is weaker than the problem assumes. The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. NOVELTY IS THE WEAK POINT and the campaign's own proof file volunteers it: the lemma is a filling construction related to classical work of Chacon-Ornstein, Rost and Thorisson - sound mathematics, very likely a known consequence.
X's law absolutely continuous with respect to Brownian motion (weaker than the problem's equivalence)
theta the unit shift with recentering on two-sided Wiener space, ergodic and invertible

title: Candidate Brownian finite-prefix embedding via forward filling
body:
CANDIDATE APPLICATION, NOT INDEPENDENTLY REVIEWED; PRIOR-LITERATURE STATUS UNVERIFIED. Burdzy-Scheutzow (2014), Problem 7.5 asks whether a process with law equivalent to Wiener measure can receive a random finite prefix to become Brownian motion. Apply the forward filling lemma on two-sided Wiener paths with theta w(t)=w(t+1)-w(1) and density f equal to the desired future-law density. The selected future W(N+t)-W(N) has the desired law; prefixing W[0,N] recovers the original Wiener path. A standard Borel disintegration supplies the coupling for an already-given suffix process. Auxiliary randomness and non-stopping joining times are essential permitted scope; no independence of prefix and suffix is asserted. The construction actually uses absolute continuity only. Check earlier filling, shift-coupling, and Brownian embedding literature before any claim of novelty.
Source Problem 7.5 permits a general random prefix
Enlargement of probability space allowed
Forward filling lemma and ergodicity of the two-sided Wiener shift

title: A randomized forward filling lemma for an ergodic stationary law
body:
Author-checked proof, not independently reviewed; novelty unassessed. If theta is an invertible measurable ergodic P-preserving map of a standard Borel probability space with measurable inverse, and Q=fP is a probability law, then on an extension with independent uniforms there is an almost surely finite N in {0,1,...} such that theta^N Z has law Q when Z~P. N can inspect the entire state and is not claimed to be a stopping time for a smaller natural filtration; no finite-mean bound is asserted. Deterministic integer shifts cannot generally do this.
Standard Borel probability space
Invertible ergodic P-preserving theta
Nonnegative integrable density f with integral one
Independent auxiliary uniforms permitted

Thus pushing hP forward under theta gives (Lh)P. Set

    a_0=1,  b_0=f,
    m_n=min(a_n,b_n),
    a_(n+1)=L(a_n-m_n),
    b_(n+1)=b_n-m_n.

All these functions are measurable and nonnegative. Inductively 0<=a_n<=1. The b_n decrease and are bounded above by f, so they have an integrable pointwise limit b_infinity. Since L preserves integrals, both remaining densities have the same mass r_n:

    integral a_n dP = integral b_n dP = r_n,
    r_n decreases to r = integral b_infinity dP,
    sum_(n>=0) integral m_n dP = 1-r.

### The remaining mass must be zero

Iteration gives the exact identity

    a_n = 1 - sum_(k=0)^(n-1) L^(n-k)m_k.

For each fixed k, the ergodic theorem for the measure-preserving transformation theta^(-1) gives

    (1/M) sum_(n=k+1)^(M-1) L^(n-k)m_k
       -> integral m_k dP

in L1(P). The L1 assertion follows from the usual almost-sure ergodic theorem and equality of the integrals for nonnegative averages, or by approximation from bounded functions. Initial omitted terms do not affect the limit.

Truncate the sum in k at K. Its tail has L1 norm at most sum_(k>=K) integral m_k dP, uniformly in M. That tail tends to zero as K grows. Therefore

    (1/M) sum_(n=0)^(M-1) a_n -> r

in L1(P), where r on the right is the constant function.

Suppose r>0. There is a delta>0 such that B={b_infinity>=delta} has positive P-measure. On B,

    m_n=min(a_n,b_n) >= min(a_n,delta)
        >= min(1,delta) a_n,

where the last step uses a_n<=1. Averaging and integrating over B gives

    liminf_M (1/M) sum_(n<M) integral_B m_n dP
        >= min(1,delta) r P(B) > 0.

But the entire sum of the integrals of m_n is at most one, so its Cesaro average tends to zero. This contradiction proves r=0. In particular sum_n m_n=f in L1 and almost everywhere.

### Realizing the matching as a random shift

Sample Z with law P and independent U_0,U_1,... uniform on [0,1]. At stage n, if not previously accepted, inspect theta^n Z and accept when

    U_n <= h_n(theta^n Z),
    h_n=m_n/a_n on {a_n>0}, and h_n=0 elsewhere.

By induction, the subprobability distribution of theta^n Z before this test is a_n P. The mass accepted at stage n has distribution m_n P, and the surviving mass pushed forward has distribution a_(n+1)P. Hence P(N>=n)=r_n tends to zero, while the law of theta^N Z is sum_n m_n P=fP=Q. Every U_n is independent of Z and of preceding U's, so the induction is valid even though h_n can inspect an entire trajectory. This proves the lemma.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b8da3914c025f776becd4c7419db38e80462225508c91d60d591f38f130c642d","revision_digest":"sha256:2b15255aa3a9ad0d5f14525fa3513e2c3fed532d5e9ecbdaa534014e943ad3e7","source_id":"owner-original-probability-research-20260906:forward-filling","source_revision":"author-checked-20260906-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

title: Brownian motion
body: Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a medium. The traditional mathematical formulation of Brownian motion is that of the Wiener process, which is often itself called "Brownian motion", even in mathematical sources.

title: Brownian Motion
body: Standard Brownian motion (the Wiener process) is a stochastic process W with W_0 = 0, independent increments, W_t - W_s distributed N(0, t - s) for s < t, and continuous paths. It exists (Wiener), is a martingale, is nowhere differentiable almost surely, has quadratic variation [W]_t = t, and is the scaling limit of random walks (Donsker).

title: Wiener Process (Standard Brownian Motion)
body: A standard Brownian motion, or Wiener process, is a real-valued stochastic process (W_t)_{t >= 0} on a probability space such that (i) W_0 = 0 almost surely; (ii) for 0 <= s < t the increment W_t - W_s is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t - s; (iii) increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; (iv) almost every sample path t |-> W_t is continuous. Existence is Wiener's theorem (constructed for instance by the Levy-Ciesielski series or as the Kolmogorov-extension limit with continuity from Kolmogorov's criterion, since E|W_t - W_s|^4 = 3 (t - s)^2). Consequences packaged with the definition: the covariance is E[W_s W_t] = min(s, t); paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable and have unbounded variation on every interval, with quadratic variation t; Brownian scaling c^{-1/2} W_{c t}, time inversion t W_{1/t}, and reflection are again Brownian motions; W is a continuous martingale and a Markov process with transition density the Gaussian kernel. Conditions (i)-(iii) characterise the finite-dimensional laws; (iv) selects the continuous version, which is the object meant in every theorem about paths.

title: Attempt on Explicit stationary law of the leftmost Hammersley drift-jump particles
body:
ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit stationary law of the leftmost Hammersley drift-jump particles structural calculation Result: The established rank representation can be expanded into a convergent combinatorial density series. Let B=(1=b1<...<bk) be the limiting first-row labels of the insertion tableau, and let q_B be its probability. The first b=bk labels form a uniform permutation, so q_B=(1/b!)*sum over partitions lambda of b with first row length k of f^lambda times the number of standard tableaux of shape lambda with first row B. Independent unit-rate Poisson spacings then give density exp(-xk)*sum_B q_B*product_(i=2..k)[(x_i-x_(i-1))^(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)/(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)!]. Check: Restriction of an insertion tableau to labels at most b is the tableau of the corresponding restricted subword. The last specified first-row entry b pins the first k labels, irrespective of later larger labels. Conditional on B, the Poisson arrival times have independent gamma increments, so every term is a normalized conditional density and nonnegative summation is valid. For k1 this gives Exp(1); known Poissonized LIS formulas give P(X2>x)=exp(-x)*I0(2sqrt(x)) and E X2=e. Obstruction: This repackages a known representation into explicit but rapidly growing finite-tableau coefficients and an infinite sum. It does not establish a new tractable closed joint law or its novelty, and should not be promoted as a full solution to the source request.

title: Connective constant
body: In mathematics, the connective constant is a numerical quantity associated with self-avoiding walks on a lattice. It is studied in connection with the notion of universality in two-dimensional statistical physics models. While the connective constant depends on the choice of lattice so itself is not universal, it is nonetheless an important quantity that appears in conjectures for universal laws. Furthermore, the mathematical techniques used to understand the connective constant, for example in the recent rigorous proof by Duminil-Copin and Smirnov that the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice has the precise value , may provide clues to a possible approach for attacking other important open problems in the study of self-avoiding walks, notably the conjecture that self-avoiding walks converge in the scaling limit to the Schramm–Loewner evolution.

title: Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746: Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant
body: [Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] For a family H of finite graphs, the k-depth connective constant of H for a fixed k, denoted by µk(H), is supG∈H µk(G). The lower connective constant of H, denoted by µinf(H), is infk≥1 µk(H). For an infinite graph G, let HG denote the set of all finite subgraphs of G. We establish the following relationship: for any infinite graph G with connective constant σ(G), µinf(HG) ≤σ(G).

title: Definition 3.1 (Log-depth connective constant [SSŠY17]) of arXiv:2604.02746: Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Co
body: [Definition 3.1 (Log-depth connective constant [SSŠY17]) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] For a family H of finite graphs, the log-depth connective constant of H, denoted by µlog(H) is at most d if there exist constants a and c such that for any graph G = (V, E) in H and any vertex v ∈V , we have N≤k(G, v) ≤cdℓ for all ℓ≥a log |V |. We provide the following counter-example to illustrate that a bound on µlog(H) does not imply a uniform zero-free region.

body: [Definition 3.5 (Connective constants for infinite graphs) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] For an infinite graph G, the connective constant σ(G) of G is lim supk→∞σk(G).

title: Attempt on Existence of the limit of e^{-alpha h} E nu(f_h) for the DGFF cluster law
body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Renewal-type argument on the cluster process viewed from the local maximum: depth-h count as a branching-like functional of the concentric decomposition. Result: Writing the cluster as the field pinned at a local maximum, e^{-alpha h} E nu(f_h) is the expected number of points at depth h weighted by e^{-alpha h}; the concentric decomposition expresses the cluster as a random walk with a Bessel-like entropic repulsion plus independent fine fields, so f_h is a sum over scales k <= log(h) of contributions, each of order e^{alpha h} times the probability that the walk is at height h at scale k. A renewal theorem for the walk under entropic repulsion would give the limit; the walk is not a true random walk (steps depend on scale through the binding fields), which is where the existing tools stop. Existence of the limit is therefore reduced to a scale-inhomogeneous renewal theorem. Obstruction: Scale inhomogeneity of the concentric-decomposition walk defeats the standard renewal theorem.

title: Attempt on The mean number of sites deep in an extremal DGFF cluster
body:
ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Integrator-authored exact restricted calculation or proof-obstruction analysis after primary-source comparison Result: Tonelli yields E[F_h]=sum_z P(phi_z<=h). For beta>alpha it also gives G(beta):=sum_z E[exp(-beta*phi_z)]=beta*integral_0^infinity exp(-beta*h)*E[F_h] dh, allowing infinite values. If the desired limit is c, the Abelian implication is (beta-alpha)*G(beta)->alpha*c as beta decreases to alpha. The converse needs more information: the increasing function f(h)=exp(alpha*h)*(1+epsilon*sin(h)), with 0<epsilon<alpha/sqrt(alpha^2+1), has the same leading Laplace pole but exp(-alpha*h)*f(h) has no limit. Thus proving a pole alone would not settle the pointwise cluster asymptotic. Check: Integrate exp(-beta*h)*1{phi_z<=h} from phi_z to infinity to obtain exp(-beta*phi_z)/beta. For the counterdiagnostic, fprime has bracket alpha+epsilon*(alpha*sin(h)+cos(h))>0, and the oscillatory Laplace term remains bounded at beta=alpha. Obstruction: No asymptotic for the actual cluster transform or a valid Tauberian remainder is established. The oscillatory function diagnoses an implication, not the DGFF conjecture.
